newsitem.title: USA: Two killed, 12 injured in Alaska climbing accident.
newsitem.headline: Two killed, 12 injured in Alaska climbing accident.

text.p: Eleven participants in a mountaineering class were in an Anchorage hospital Monday and two others were dead after an Alaska climbing expedition fell 1,000 feet (300-metres) down a steep gully.
Killed were Steven Brown, 23, and Mary Fogarty, 40, both of Anchorage.

A dozen students and two instructors from the University of Alaska Anchorage wilderness education programme were roped together and descending the 4,880-foot (1,487-metre) Ptarmigan Peak in Anchorage's Chugach State Park late on Sunday when one climber lost control and triggered a tumble by the others, Steve Wilhelmi, spokesman for the Alaska State Troopers, said.
"They were all roped together when one of them slipped and fell, and that resulted in the whole group going down," Wilhelmi told reporters gathered at the park trailhead closest to the accident site.
The climbers started their slide on a snowfield, then crossed hard ice and landed in a field of boulders, Wilhelmi said.

The troopers, Chugach State Park rangers and other officials closed that section of the park on Sunday evening and spent the next several hours coordinating a helicopter rescue that ferried the injured from the steep mountain slope to an Anchorage hospital.
Other weekend visitors to the mountainous park, a busy centre for recreation, helped in the rescue.
One of the first on the scene was 14-year-old Aaron Medlock, who was bicycling with his family on a trail along Ptarmigan Peak's base.

The family used a cellular telephone to call for help and began applying first aid to the climbers, who were "totally still" except for one who was able to walk, the teenager said. At least one was dead then, he said.
Matthew Medlock, 12, said he was shielded from the scene. "My brother told me it was really gory and I would get nightmares," he said after emerging from the trail.

The north-facing gully where the climbers fell is popular with back-country skiers during the winter but treacherous in the summer and fall, when its blanket of soft snow disappears, Marc Esslinger, an assistant state park ranger, said.
"It's year-round snow and ice, mostly ice," he said. "It's a steep area. It's a really gnarly ice gully."
Most of the injured -- among whom were the class's two instructors -- were listed in fair condition with fractures, internal injuries, cuts and other ailments.
One climber was in serious condition. The sole remaining member of the party was treated and released. All were from Anchorage or nearby communities.
